l3-cbet: A C-Bet (Continuation Bet) is when the last preflop raiser continues betting on the flop. For example, you raise preflop, an opponent calls, and you're first to bet on the flop — that's a C-Bet.
The core logic of the C-Bet: most of the time the flop doesn't help either player much. As the preflop aggressor, you have a range advantage.

Standard C-Bet size: 50-75% of the pot
Dry boards (e.g. K-7-2 rainbow): 33-50% pot
Wet boards (e.g. J-T-9 two-tone): 66-75% pot
Don't C-Bet 100% of the time. The right approach is to C-Bet on favorable boards and Check on unfavorable ones. Cultivate "selective aggression".

C-Bet EV formula (including fold equity and showdown equity):
Bet EV = opponent fold rate × current pot + (1-fold rate) × (equity × new pot - loss rate × bet size)

Example: pot 6BB, C-Bet 4BB, fold rate 40%, equity 20%
EV = 0.4×6 + 0.6×(0.2×14 - 0.8×4) = 2.4 + 0.6×(2.8-3.2) = 2.4 - 0.24 = +2.16BB

Theory reference: the theoretical analysis of C-Bet EV construction and betting purposes is in Theory Academy T5 Chapter 2 "GTO vs Exploitative: Two Kinds of Optimal" and T6 Chapter 1 "Betting Purposes". Under the GTO framework, C-Bet frequency and range selection are closely related.

Counter-intuitive: a C-Bet doesn't need a strong hand. As long as you have enough fold equity (the opponent folds often enough), even if your hand completely missed the board, the C-Bet is still +EV. That's why GTO strategies can C-Bet at up to 60-70% frequency, including plenty of bluffs.
l3-draws:
Flush draw: 9 outs, about 35% equity (flop to river)
Open-ended straight draw: 8 outs, about 31% equity
Gutshot straight draw: 4 outs, about 16% equity
Two overcards: 6 outs (pairing either overcard)

Passive play (recommended for beginners): call to see the next card, seeing more cards at minimum cost
Semi-bluff (advanced): bet/raise with a draw, gaining fold equity
All-in: when the pot odds are good enough
Always calculate pot odds! If your equity > pot odds, calling is +EV.
Pros choose their draw line based on position and opponent tendencies. Semi-bluffing with draws from position is a very effective strategy.

The 2/4 Rule and error analysis:
One card (turn): equity ≈ Outs × 2%
Two cards (all-in on flop): equity ≈ Outs × 4%

Error analysis (flop→river two-card scenario):
4 Outs (gutshot): ×4 estimates 16% | exact 16.5% | error -0.5
8 Outs (OESD): ×4 estimates 32% | exact 31.4% | error +0.6
9 Outs (flush): ×4 estimates 36% | exact 35.0% | error +1.0
12 Outs (combo draw): ×4 estimates 48% | exact 45.0% | error +3.0

Conclusion: for Outs ≤ 9, ×4 has error within 1 percentage point; for Outs ≥ 13, use the corrected formula.

Theory reference: the full derivation of Outs counting and the 2/4 Rule is in Theory Academy T1 Chapter 2 "Outs and the 2/4 Rule", including the error analysis table and corrected formula. The EV framework for calling with draws is in T2 Chapter 1.

Counter-intuitive: combo draws (flush + straight + overcards) have far more equity than intuition suggests. For example, J♥T♥ on a 9♥8♦3♣ board has 15 outs and about 54% equity — actually ahead of most one-pair hands. That's why combo draws are the best semi-bluff candidates.
l3-multistreet: Multi-Street Planning means planning the turn/river strategy while making your flop decision. Not "one street at a time", but "how many streets do I plan to play this hand? Which boards do I continue on? Which boards do I give up on?"
Double Barrel = flop C-Bet + turn continuation bet. Frequency about 50-60%, depending on board structure and opponent.

Continue barreling: 1) the turn improves your hand (top pair/draw completes) 2) the turn is a "blank" (doesn't change the board structure) 3) the opponent folds to turn bets at a high rate. Give up: 1) the turn completes an obvious draw 2) the opponent raises/donks the turn 3) your hand gains no equity.
Triple Barrel (river all-in bluff) conditions: 1) polarized range (strong hands or pure bluffs) 2) you have Blockers 3) the opponent is not a Calling Station.
Delayed C-Bet: check the flop, bet the turn. Use when: 1) the flop isn't suited to a C-Bet 2) you want to see showdown cheaply 3) the opponent leads the turn frequently after checking the flop.

SPR (Stack-to-Pot Ratio) formula:
SPR = effective stack ÷ pot size

SPR tiers and strategy lean:
SPR < 4 (low): committed play — top pair can get all-in comfortably
SPR 4-10 (medium): standard play, be careful
SPR > 10 (high): deep stacks — speculative hands like suited connectors gain value

Geometric sizing over three streets:
Ideal three-street all-in → about 60-70% pot each street
Example: pot 6BB, effective 100BB, SPR≈17
Flop bet 4BB → pot 14BB
Turn bet 10BB → pot 34BB
River bet 25BB → pot 84BB, total bet 39BB ≈ 40% of effective stack

Theory reference: the full derivation of SPR and geometric sizing is in Theory Academy T6 Chapter 3 "SPR and Three-Street Geometric Sizing". Betting plans in multi-street play are closely tied to range construction.

Counter-intuitive: at deep stacks (SPR > 10), small suited connectors are worth more than big pairs. AA's postflop realization drops at deep stacks because opponents can apply pressure with wider ranges on later streets, while hands like 98s have better postflop playability and can make many strong hands.
l3-checkraise: Check-Raise = check first, then raise when the opponent bets. Value Check-Raise: two pair+/Set on wet boards (protect a strong hand + build a big pot). Bluff Check-Raise: strong draws (combo flush+straight draws with equity + fold equity).
BB vs C-Bet Check-Raise frequency is about 10-15%. The range should be balanced: value hands (Set/two pair/strong top pair) + Bluffs (combo draws/strong draws).
Fold: weak/marginal hands (middle pair/weak top pair). Call: strong but not the nuts (top pair good kicker/overpair). Re-Raise: the nuts (Set+/two pair+) or strong bluffs (combo draws).
Check-Raise size: usually 2.5-3x the C-Bet. Example: C-Bet 4BB → Check-Raise 10-12BB.

Don't Check-Raise bluff frequently on dry boards. On dry boards (e.g. K-7-2 rainbow) the opponent's C-Bet range is strong, so the Check-Raise fold rate is low. Wet boards (e.g. J-T-9 two-tone) are better.
l3-float-probe: Float = call the C-Bet on the flop, planning to bet the turn when the opponent checks, to steal the pot. Use when: 1) the opponent C-Bets often but gives up on the turn a lot 2) you have position 3) the board suits bluffing (dry board/weak opponent range).
Float hand selection: backdoor draws (backdoor flush/straight), overcards (A/K high), weak pairs (bottom/middle pair). Pure air is not suited to floating.

Probe Bet = you bet the turn after the preflop raiser checks the flop. Use when: 1) the opponent checks the flop frequently 2) the opponent folds to turn bets at a high rate 3) you have some equity (not pure air).
Float vs Probe difference: Float is betting the turn after calling a C-Bet; Probe is betting the turn after the opponent checks the flop. Both exploit position + opponent weaknesses.
Don't Float/Probe against a Calling Station. CS won't fold — you're just donating money. These strategies target opponents who can fold, like TAGs and NITs.
l3-bet-sizing: Small (25-33% pot): dry boards/range advantage. Medium (50-66% pot): standard value bets. Large (75-100% pot): wet boards/polarized ranges. Overbet (125-200% pot): river nut-advantage boards (a core modern GTO concept).
Bet size vs range: small bet = wide range (many hands can bet) | large bet = narrow range (only strong hands or pure bluffs).

Small: dry boards (K-7-2 rainbow)/range advantage (preflop raiser vs BB). Medium: standard value bets (top pair/overpair). Large: wet boards (J-T-9 two-tone)/when protecting strong hands. Overbet: river polarized ranges (nuts or air)/when the opponent's range is capped.

The Overbet is a core modern GTO concept. When you have the nut advantage on the river (e.g. flush-completing board), use an Overbet to put maximum pressure on the opponent and force medium-strength hands into tough decisions.
Don't use a fixed bet size (e.g. always 50% pot). Adjust based on board structure, range advantage, and opponent type. Varied sizing makes it hard for opponents to read your hand strength.

MDF (Minimum Defense Frequency) formula:
MDF = pot ÷ (pot + bet)
Alpha (opponent's bluff break-even point) formula:
Alpha = bet ÷ (pot + bet)

Common values:
1/3 pot bet → MDF=75%, Alpha=25%
1/2 pot bet → MDF=67%, Alpha=33%
2/3 pot bet → MDF=60%, Alpha=40%
Full pot bet → MDF=50%, Alpha=50%

Note: MDF is the defense frequency and Alpha is the minimum fold rate a bluff needs — they are complements (MDF + Alpha = 1).

Theory reference: the algebraic derivation of MDF and Alpha is in Theory Academy T5 Chapter 3 "Minimum Defense Frequency (MDF) and Alpha". The mathematical basis of bet sizing and geometric sizing is in T6 Chapter 2.

Counter-intuitive: the bigger your bet, the more opponents fold — but your bluff needs a higher success rate. A big bet means you risk more to win a limited pot. With a full-pot bet your bluff needs at least 50% fold rate to break even, while a half-pot bet only needs 33%.
l3-bluffing:
Bluffing isn't "stealing" — it's a +EV decision with rigorous mathematical foundations.

Fold Equity formula:
FE = opponent fold probability × pot size

Bluff break-even point:
When the opponent's fold rate > bet / (pot + bet), the bluff is +EV.

Example: bet 2/3 pot → need fold rate > 40%
Bet 1/2 pot → need fold rate > 33%
Bet pot → need fold rate > 50%
Core formula: Bluff EV = Fold% × Pot - Call% × Bet. When Fold% > Bet/(Pot+Bet), a pure bluff is +EV even without considering postflop implied odds.

Flop bluffs: highest frequency (opponent's range is widest, hit rate lowest), small size works (33-50% pot).

Turn bluffs: frequency drops; you need better blockers or a consistent narrative (your action line must represent a strong hand). Turn barrels usually use 60-75% pot.

River bluffs: most cautious, only in polarized spots (nuts or air). The river has no implied odds — pure fold equity — so you need enough foldable combos in the opponent's range.
Three-street bluff frequency decreasing principle: Flop > Turn > River. Each continued barrel needs a stronger reason (better blockers, more consistent narrative, weaker opponent range).

Definition: bet/raise with a draw (not currently ahead but with outs to improve).

Two ways to profit:
1. Opponent folds → win the pot directly (Fold Equity)
2. Opponent calls → hit and win a big pot (Equity Realization)

Semi-Bluff EV = Fold% × Pot + Call% × Equity × (Pot + Bet) - Call% × (1-Equity) × Bet

Best Semi-Bluff hand ranking:
Combo draws (flush+straight) > flush draws > open-ended straight draws > gutshots
The Semi-Bluff is the safest bluff form for beginners — even when called, you still have outs to improve. Always prefer bluffing with hands that have equity.

Big bets (75-150% pot) → polarized range (nuts + bluffs, no medium hands)
Small bets (25-33% pot) → merged range (wide range with thin value)

Key principle: bluff size should match value-bet size.
If you value-bet 75% pot, your bluffs should also be 75% pot.
Inconsistent sizing exposes your hand strength (read by opponents).

River theoretical ratio: for every 1 value bet, add 1/(pot_odds+1) bluffs.

Example: bet pot (opponent needs 33% equity to call) → bluff:value = 1:2
Bet 1/2 pot (opponent needs 25% equity) → bluff:value = 1:3

In practice slightly below the theoretical ratio (because opponents overcall and low-stakes opponents don't fold enough).

Easy memory: bet pot on the river → 1 in 3 bets is a bluff.
l3-texture: Board texture refers to the structural characteristics of the community cards: connectivity, suit distribution, high/low cards, etc. Different textures require completely different strategies.

Dry board (e.g. K♠72A♠):
• Few draws or combinations
• The preflop raiser has a big range advantage
• Suits small continuation bets (1/3 pot)
• Turn/river strategy changes little

Wet board (e.g. 9♠8♠7♣):
• Many draws, straights, flushes
• The defender's range hits hard
• Suits big bets to protect made hands (2/3-full pot)
• The turn can completely change the situation

1. Connectedness: does the board form straights/straight draws
2. Suitedness: is there a flush/flush draw
3. High/Low: is the board high cards or low cards
High-card dry boards (e.g. AK2r) favor the preflop raiser; low-card wet boards (e.g. 876ss) favor the caller. Decide whether to bet based on who has the bigger range advantage.
On wet boards, your "unimproved strong hand" can become second-best by the turn. Either bet strongly to protect, or be ready to fold.
l3-check-range: Why Do You Need a Checking Range?
If you always bet with strong hands and check with weak ones, opponents easily read your strategy. Building a balanced checking range is key to protecting yourself from exploitation.
Core principle: your checking range should include some strong hands (for Check-Raises or later-street action), not only weak hands.
When to Check Instead of Bet

Check is appropriate when:
1. You have no range advantage (e.g. low-card boards out of position)
2. You have medium-strength hands and want to control pot size
3. You plan to trap with a Check-Raise
4. Your strong hand needs no protection on this board
5. You're not the last to act in a multiway pot

A good checking range includes:
• Strong hands (about 15-20%): for Check-Raises or slowplay
• Medium hands (about 40-50%): control the pot, observe on later streets
• Weak/give-up hands (about 30-40%): ready to fold to a bet
If your checking range is all weak hands, opponents can attack your checks endlessly. Keeping some strong hands in your checking range is the key to defense.
Out of position (OOP), your checking range should be wider than in position (IP), because you must decide without knowing the opponent's action.
l3-3bet-postflop:
3-Bet pots are fundamentally different from single-raised pots. Because the preflop pot is bigger, the postflop SPR (Stack-to-Pot Ratio) drops significantly. This means:

- The effective stack is smaller relative to the pot, compressing decision space
- The range is narrower (a 3-Bet range is far narrower than an opening range)
- Each decision has a bigger EV impact
- It's easier to get all-in on the flop (SPR usually 3-6)
Core concept: the SPR in a 3-Bet pot is usually 3-6, far below the 8-15 of a single-raised pot. Low SPR means top-pair-strength hands are enough to stack off.

In 3-Bet pots, board classification matters more:

Overconnected (Wet/Connected): e.g. J♠T♠9♣, 8♥7♥6♣
- Very favorable to the defender's range
- The 3-Better should lower C-Bet frequency
- Overpairs like AA/KK need caution

Safe (Dry/Static): e.g. A♠7♣2♦, K♣8♥3♠
- Favorable to the 3-Better's range (many high cards)
- C-Bet frequently
- Overpairs are still the strongest hands
Common Scenario: Big Pairs in 3-Bet Pots

Postflop strategy for AA/KK in a 3-Bet pot:

1. Dry board (A-high or K-high): confident value betting, ready to stack off
2. Medium-connected board (e.g. Q-J-7): C-Bet but slow down against resistance
3. Wet-connected board (e.g. T-9-8 two-tone): Check to control the pot, give up over-aggression

Remember: in 3-Bet pots the SPR is low, so top pair good kicker is usually enough to stack off. But on wet boards beware of two pair+ hands.
The most common 3-Bet pot mistake is clinging too hard to an overpair on a wet board. AA on a J-T-9 two-tone board is only worth a Check — don't bet big just to "protect".
Key formula: SPR = effective stack ÷ pot size. When SPR < 4, top-pair strength can comfortably get all-in. When SPR > 6, you need a stronger hand to stack off.

l3-cbet-q1.question: What is a C-Bet?
options: The preflop raiser continues betting postflop
l3-cbet-q1.explanation: A C-Bet is the last preflop raiser continuing to bet on the flop.

l3-cbet-q2.question: How big should you C-Bet on a dry board (K-7-2 rainbow)?
l3-cbet-q2.explanation: Use a smaller C-Bet (33-50% pot) on dry boards, because opponents rarely have strong hands to resist with.

l3-cbet-q3.question: How big should you C-Bet on a wet board (J-T-9 two-tone)?
l3-cbet-q3.explanation: Wet boards have many draws — use a bigger bet (66-75% pot) to make draws pay.

l3-cbet-q4.question: When should you NOT C-Bet?
options: When the board favors the opponent's range
l3-cbet-q4.explanation: When the board favors the opponent's range (e.g. wet-connected boards), Check instead of C-Bet.

l3-cbet-q5.question: What is the core logic of the C-Bet?
options: The preflop raiser has range advantage
l3-cbet-q5.explanation: The core logic is that the preflop raiser usually has a range advantage, because most flops don't help either player much.

l3-draw-q1.question: How many outs does a flush draw have?
l3-draw-q1.explanation: A flush draw has 9 outs (13 suited cards - 4 known = 9 unseen suited cards).

l3-draw-q2.question: What is the recommended way for beginners to play a flush draw?
l3-draw-q2.explanation: Beginners should use passive play (calling) to see the next card at minimum cost. Semi-bluffing comes later.

l3-draw-q3.question: How many outs does an open-ended straight draw (OESD) have?
l3-draw-q3.explanation: An OESD can complete at either end, 4 cards each — 8 outs total.

l3-draw-q4.question: Using the 2/4 rule, what hit rate do 9 outs have from flop to turn?
l3-draw-q4.explanation: 2/4 rule: flop to turn uses ×2, 9×2=18%, actual about 19%.

l3-draw-q5.question: About how many outs does a combo draw (flush + OESD) have?
l3-draw-q5.explanation: 9 flush outs + 8 OESD outs, deduplicated to about 15. This is the strongest draw type.

l3-multi-q1.question: What is the core of multi-street thinking?
options: Only look at the current street
Plan the turn/river while deciding the flop
l3-multi-q1.explanation: Multi-street thinking requires planning the turn/river during the flop decision, not one street at a time.

l3-multi-q2.question: What does Double Barrel mean?
options: Check the flop + bet the turn
C-Bet the flop + continue betting the turn
Bet the flop, turn and river
l3-multi-q2.explanation: Double Barrel = flop C-Bet + turn continuation bet, the standard way for the preflop raiser to keep pressure on.

l3-multi-q3.question: What are the best conditions for a Triple Barrel bluff?
l3-multi-q3.explanation: A Triple Barrel bluff needs a polarized range + Blockers to force tough decisions.

l3-multi-q4.question: When is a Delayed C-Bet appropriate?
options: When the flop suits a C-Bet
When the flop doesn't suit a C-Bet
l3-multi-q4.explanation: A Delayed C-Bet fits when the flop isn't suited to a C-Bet, e.g. when the board favors the opponent's range.

l3-multi-q5.question: When should you give up the Double Barrel on the turn?
options: The turn completes an obvious draw
l3-multi-q5.explanation: Give up barreling when the turn completes an obvious draw, because the opponent's draw likely got there.

l3-cr-q1.question: What is a Check-Raise?
options: Check first, then raise against the opponent's bet
l3-cr-q1.explanation: Check-Raise = check first, then raise when the opponent bets — the most powerful postflop attacking weapon.

l3-cr-q2.question: What is the standard BB vs C-Bet Check-Raise frequency?
l3-cr-q2.explanation: BB vs C-Bet Check-Raise frequency is about 10-15%, with a balanced range (value + Bluffs).

l3-cr-q3.question: Which hand is best for a Check-Raise Bluff?
l3-cr-q3.explanation: A combo flush+straight draw has about 12 outs (40%+ equity) — the best Check-Raise bluff hand.

l3-cr-q4.question: How big is a typical Check-Raise relative to the C-Bet?
l3-cr-q4.explanation: A Check-Raise is usually 2.5-3x the C-Bet, e.g. C-Bet 4BB → Check-Raise 10-12BB.

l3-cr-q5.question: When should you NOT Check-Raise bluff on a dry board?
options: When the opponent's C-Bet range is strong
When the opponent folds a lot
When you have a combo draw
l3-cr-q5.explanation: On dry boards the opponent's C-Bet range is strong (e.g. K-7-2 rainbow) — the Check-Raise fold rate is low, so bluffing doesn't work.

l3-fp-q1.question: What is a Float?
options: Call the flop C-Bet, planning to steal the turn
l3-fp-q1.explanation: Float = call the C-Bet on the flop, then bet the turn when the opponent checks, to steal the pot.

l3-fp-q2.question: When is a Probe Bet appropriate?
options: After the opponent C-Bets the flop
When the preflop raiser checks the flop, you bet the turn
l3-fp-q2.explanation: Probe Bet = after the preflop raiser checks the flop, you bet the turn to steal the pot.

l3-fp-q3.question: Which opponent is the worst to Float against?
l3-fp-q3.explanation: A Calling Station won't fold (Fold to C-Bet only 20%) — floating is pure loss.

l3-fp-q4.question: What hands should you Float with?
l3-fp-q4.explanation: Float with backdoor draws, overcards, or weak pairs. Pure air is not suited to floating.

l3-fp-q5.question: What is the main difference between Probe Bet and Float?
options: Probe is betting the turn after the opponent checks the flop
l3-fp-q5.explanation: Probe Bet is betting the turn after the preflop raiser checks the flop. Float is betting the turn after calling a C-Bet when the opponent checks.

l3-bs-q1.question: What bet size should you use on a dry board (e.g. K-7-2 rainbow)?
l3-bs-q1.explanation: On dry boards you have a big range advantage — a small bet folds weak hands and gets value from strong ones.

l3-bs-q2.question: When is an Overbet most appropriate?
l3-bs-q2.explanation: The Overbet is best when you have the nut advantage on the river (e.g. flush-completing board), applying maximum pressure with a polarized range.

l3-bs-q3.question: What is the relationship between bet size and range?
options: Small bet = narrow range, big bet = wide range
Small bet = wide range, big bet = narrow range
l3-bs-q3.explanation: A small bet corresponds to a wide range (many hands can bet); a big bet corresponds to a narrow range (only strong hands or pure bluffs).

l3-bs-q4.question: When is a medium bet (50-66% pot) appropriate?
l3-bs-q4.explanation: A medium bet (50-66% pot) is the standard value-bet size for medium-strength hands like top pair/overpair.

l3-bs-q5.question: Why shouldn't you use a fixed bet size?
l3-bs-q5.explanation: A fixed size lets opponents easily read your hand strength. Varied sizing makes it hard to judge.

l3-bluff-q1.question: Betting 2/3 pot, what minimum fold rate does the opponent need for the bluff to break even?
l3-bluff-q1.explanation: Break-even formula: bet/(pot+bet) = (2/3)/(1+2/3) = 0.4 = 40%. If the opponent folds > 40%, the bluff is +EV.

l3-bluff-q2.question: Which hand is the best Semi-Bluff candidate?
l3-bluff-q2.explanation: Combo draws (flush+straight) have the most outs (about 15) and high improving odds even when called — the best Semi-Bluff hands.

l3-bluff-q3.question: Betting pot on the river, what is the theoretical bluff-to-value ratio?
l3-bluff-q3.explanation: Betting pot means the opponent needs 33% equity to call. The theoretical ratio is bluff:value = 1:2 (1 bluff for every 2 value bets).

l3-bluff-q4.question: Which street should have the highest bluff frequency?
l3-bluff-q4.explanation: On the flop the opponent's range is widest and hit rate lowest, so bluffs succeed most. As streets progress, the opponent's range strengthens and bluff frequency should decline.

l3-bluff-q5.question: What are the two ways a Semi-Bluff profits?
options: Opponent folds + hitting a big pot
l3-bluff-q5.explanation: A Semi-Bluff profits by the opponent folding (winning the pot directly) or by hitting when called (winning a big pot).

l3-texture-q1.question: Which of these is a "dry board"?
l3-texture-q1.explanation: K♠72♠ has no connectivity, no flush, scattered high/low cards — a classic dry board.

l3-texture-q2.question: How should bet size adjust on a wet board?
l3-texture-q2.explanation: On wet boards opponents have many draws — bet big to make them pay to continue.

l3-texture-q3.question: Who does a high-card dry board favor?
l3-texture-q3.explanation: High-card dry boards (e.g. AK2) hit the preflop raiser's range more, because that range has more big cards.

l3-texture-q4.question: What are the three dimensions of board texture?
l3-texture-q4.explanation: The three dimensions are connectivity, suit distribution, and high/low cards.

l3-texture-q5.question: Who does a low-card wet board (e.g. 876ss) favor?
l3-texture-q5.explanation: Low-card wet boards favor the caller, because such boards hit the caller's range more.

l3-check-range-q1.question: What should a checking range contain?
l3-check-range-q1.explanation: A balanced checking range mixes hand strengths so opponents can't easily read your strategy.

l3-check-range-q2.question: Which situation is NOT suited to checking?
options: Low-card board with no range advantage
In position with a clear range advantage
l3-check-range-q2.explanation: In position with a clear range advantage, you should bet for value rather than give a free card.

l3-check-range-q3.question: How should the OOP checking range compare to IP?
l3-check-range-q3.explanation: OOP lacks information and needs a wider checking range to balance strategy and avoid being read.

l3-check-range-q4.question: What are the strong hands in the checking range for?
l3-check-range-q4.explanation: Strong hands in the checking range serve Check-Raise traps or slowplay, stopping opponents from easily reading your strategy.

l3-check-range-q5.question: When should you bet instead of check?
options: In position with a clear range advantage
l3-check-range-q5.explanation: In position with a clear range advantage, bet for value rather than giving a free card.

l3-3bet-pf-q1.question: What SPR range do 3-Bet pots usually have?
l3-3bet-pf-q1.explanation: Because the preflop pot is bigger, the SPR in a 3-Bet pot is usually 3-6, far below a single-raised pot.

l3-3bet-pf-q2.question: In a 3-Bet pot with SPR 3, how should top pair typically be played?
options: Control the pot, one street only
l3-3bet-pf-q2.explanation: When SPR < 4, top-pair strength can comfortably get all-in, because the stack is already shallow relative to the pot.

l3-3bet-pf-q3.question: What should AA do on a J-T-9 two-tone board in a 3-Bet pot?
l3-3bet-pf-q3.explanation: J-T-9 two-tone is an overconnected board that strongly favors the defender. AA is an overpair but should Check to control the pot and avoid being trapped by two pair/straights.

l3-3bet-pf-q4.question: Which board favors the 3-Better most?
l3-3bet-pf-q4.explanation: A-7-2 rainbow is a dry board that most favors the 3-Better's range (many high Ax) — C-Bet frequently.

l3-3bet-pf-q5.question: What is the main effect of low SPR in a 3-Bet pot?
l3-3bet-pf-q5.explanation: Low SPR compresses decision space — top pair can often get all-in, making postflop decisions relatively simpler.

l3-cbet-ex1.title: Dry board C-Bet: small size, high frequency
reasoning: K-7-2 rainbow is a very dry board
The opponent rarely hits this board — a small bet gets folds
You have A-high, so even when called you have 6 outs
A 33% pot C-Bet offers the best value
l3-cbet-ex1.mistakeReasoning: Betting big on a dry board is wasteful. The opponent either folds or has a strong hand — a big bet gains no extra value.
l3-cbet-ex1.tableDesc: Standard 100BB cash game; the opponent called your BTN open preflop

l3-cbet-ex2.title: Wet board Check: don't attack an unfavorable board
reasoning: J-T-9 two-tone is a very wet board
BTN's calling range contains many two pairs, straights, and draws
You only have A-high with no pair
This board favors the opponent's range — a C-Bet gets called or raised a lot
l3-cbet-ex2.mistakeReasoning: C-Betting with air on a wet board is a serious mistake. The opponent has too many strong hands and draws that continue — your bluff rarely works.
l3-cbet-ex2.tableDesc: The BTN is a LAG player who called with a very wide range preflop

l3-draws-ex1.title: Flush draw calling decision
reasoning: You have an A-high flush draw (9 outs)
About 35% equity from flop to river
Opponent C-Bets 4BB, pot is 10.5BB — you only need to call 4BB
Pot odds = 4/14.5 ≈ 28%, your equity 35% > 28% — calling is +EV
l3-draws-ex1.mistakeReasoning: A flush draw has 35% equity and great pot odds — folding is a serious -EV error. You're giving up huge equity.

l3-draws-ex2.title: Semi-bluff raise: combo draw
reasoning: You have a flush draw + open-ended straight draw (combo draw)
Combo draws have about 12-15 outs (9 flush + 8 straight, deduplicated), about 45-54% equity
Raising gains both fold equity and made-hand value
Even when called, you still have high equity
l3-draws-ex2.mistakeReasoning: Combo draws have huge equity — raise to build the pot actively. Only calling wastes fold equity and initiative.
l3-draws-ex2.tableDesc: The CO is a NIT with a very high fold-to-raise rate (70%)

l3-multi-ex1.title: Double Barrel: top pair continues on the turn
reasoning: After the flop C-Bet CO calls, the turn 2♠ is a blank
AK top pair top kicker — continue barreling on the turn for value
TAG's flop calling range: Ax/9x/draws — many will continue calling
2♠ doesn't change the board structure — your hand is still ahead
l3-multi-ex1.mistakeReasoning: Checking top pair top kicker on the turn is too passive. On a blank continue barreling for value.

l3-multi-ex2.title: Give-Up: giving up the bluff on the turn
reasoning: After the flop C-Bet CS calls, the turn T♥ may complete draws
QJ gains no equity — continuing to barrel against a CS is -EV
CS won't fold (Fold to C-Bet only 20%) — the bluff is useless
Check to control the pot and see if the river improves you
l3-multi-ex2.mistakeReasoning: Continuing to bluff a Calling Station is pure loss. CS won't fold — you're just donating money.

l3-cr-ex1.title: Value Check-Raise: Set on a wet board
reasoning: Set of 9s on a J-9-8 two-tone board should Check-Raise
Wet boards have many draws — protect your strong hand
LAG C-Bets at high frequency (80%) — the Check-Raise gains value
Build a big pot to set up a turn/river shove
l3-cr-ex1.mistakeReasoning: Only calling with a Set on a wet board is too passive. Check-Raise to build the pot + protect.

l3-cr-ex2.title: Bluff Check-Raise: combo draw
reasoning: J♥T♥ on a 9-8-4 two-tone board has a flush + gutshot combo draw
About 12 outs (40%+ equity) — Check-Raise semi-bluff
TAG folds to Check-Raises at a high rate
Even when called you have high equity and can continue on the turn/river
l3-cr-ex2.mistakeReasoning: Only calling with a combo draw wastes fold equity + initiative. A Check-Raise semi-bluff is more +EV.

l3-fp-ex1.title: Float: steal the pot on the turn after calling the C-Bet
reasoning: Called the flop C-Bet (Float), then CO checks the turn
TAG checking the turn indicates a weak hand (below top pair)
QJ has backdoor straight potential + overcard equity
A turn bet represents Kx — TAG folds weak hands
l3-fp-ex1.mistakeReasoning: Checking the turn misses the steal opportunity. TAG's check signals weakness — bet to pressure.

l3-fp-ex2.title: Probe Bet: bet the turn after the opponent checks the flop
reasoning: Both check the flop, then NIT checks the turn again
NIT checking twice indicates extreme weakness
AT has overcard equity + backdoor flush potential
A Probe bet represents 9x/6x — NIT folds air
l3-fp-ex2.mistakeReasoning: NIT checking twice is a clear weakness signal — Probe to steal. Checking misses the opportunity.

l3-bs-ex1.title: Small bet: dry board range advantage
reasoning: K-7-2 rainbow is an extremely dry board — BB's range rarely hits
BTN has a huge range advantage — C-Bet small and often
A small bet (33% pot) folds weak hands and gets calls from strong ones
No need to protect with a big bet — there are no draws
l3-bs-ex1.mistakeReasoning: Betting big on a dry board is wasteful. A small bet achieves the goal; a big bet folds all weak hands and gains no value.

l3-bs-ex2.title: Overbet: river polarized range
reasoning: The river 7♥ completes the flush — BTN has the nut flush (A♥Q♥)
BB's range is capped (no A♥, at best a K♥x flush)
The Overbet (160% pot) puts maximum pressure on BB
Polarized range: nut flush or pure bluff — the Overbet is the standard size
l3-bs-ex2.mistakeReasoning: Using only 60% pot with the nut flush is wasteful. An Overbet gets maximum value — BB calls with weaker flushes.

l3-bluff-ex1.title: River polarized-spot bluff
reasoning: AQ is only A-high (top pair weak kicker) here, but your range is polarized
Three streets of betting represent AK/AA/KK etc. super strong hands
BB's calling range is squeezed to A-kicker/two pair — many fold to a pot bet
A-high has no showdown value (BB has Kx/Ax stronger) — bluffing is the only way to win
Fold equity: TAG folds to a three-street pot bet about 55-60%
l3-bluff-ex1.mistakeReasoning: Checking almost certainly loses (A-high has minimal showdown value). With a consistent three-street narrative, the river bluff is +EV. Giving up wastes the image built on the first two streets.

l3-bluff-ex2.title: Flop semi-bluff: raising the C-Bet with a flush draw
reasoning: T♥9♥ is a flush draw (9 outs) + gutshot potential (J completes a straight)
Raising the C-Bet is a semi-bluff: the opponent may fold (Fold Equity)
Even when called, you have about 35% equity (9 flush outs + partial straight outs)
On a K-high board, your raise represents Kx/set — consistent narrative
BTN C-Bets often but folds to raises about 45%
l3-bluff-ex2.mistakeReasoning: Calling isn't losing, but it forfeits fold equity. A semi-bluff raise has one more way to win (opponent folds), with about +1.5BB/100 higher EV than passive calling.

l3-3bet-pf-ex1.title: AA on a dry board in a 3-Bet pot
reasoning: A-7-2 rainbow is an extremely dry board — very favorable to the 3-Better
AA is the nuts level — at SPR 4.3 it can fully stack off
TAG's range contains Ax/medium pairs that will call
A 50% pot bet gains value without scaring off all weak hands
l3-3bet-pf-ex1.mistakeReasoning: Slowplaying on a dry board is unnecessary. The SPR is low — bet directly to build the pot.
l3-3bet-pf-ex1.tableDesc: Standard 100BB cash game; 3Bet pot with SPR around 4.3

l3-3bet-pf-ex2.title: KK on a wet board in a 3-Bet pot
reasoning: Q-J-8 two-tone is an overconnected board — very favorable to CO's defense range
TAG's range contains many QJ/TT/99/flush draws
KK is an overpair but very vulnerable
Check to control the pot — if facing a bet, consider calling one street but not stacking off
l3-3bet-pf-ex2.mistakeReasoning: Big C-Betting on an overconnected board is a serious mistake. When called you're almost always behind; when raised you face a tough decision.
l3-3bet-pf-ex2.tableDesc: Standard 100BB cash game; 3Bet pot with SPR around 4.1

d-l3-cbet-q1.question: You open BTN, BB calls. Flop: K♠ 7♥ 2♣. You hold AK — what should you do?

d-l3-odds-q1.scenario: Flop, you have AK two overcards (4 outs)
d-l3-odds-q1.question: AK two overcards (4 outs): what is the hit rate from Flop to Turn?
d-l3-odds-q1.explanation: Flop→Turn single-street probability ≈ outs/47 = 4/47 ≈ 8.5%, rounded to about 9%. Note: the "2/4 rule" estimates two-street cumulative probability, not a single street.

d-l3-odds-q2.scenario: Flop, you have a flush draw
d-l3-odds-q2.question: A flush draw (9 outs) from Flop to River hits about how often?
d-l3-odds-q2.explanation: 9 outs flop to river: 2/4 rule 9×4=36%, actual about 35%. This is one of the most important odds calculations.

d-l3-odds-q3.question: An OESD (8 outs) from Flop to River hits about how often?
d-l3-odds-q3.explanation: 8 outs with the 2/4 rule: 8×4=32%. Actual about 31.5%. OESD is the strongest draw besides a flush draw.

d-l3-odds-q4.scenario: Turn, you have a flush draw
d-l3-odds-q4.question: A flush draw (9 outs) from Turn to River hits about how often?
d-l3-odds-q4.explanation: Turn to river is only one card: 9/46 ≈ 19.6%. Using 2×2: 9×2=18%, close to the actual value.

d-l3-odds-q5.question: Pot is 15BB, you need to call 5BB. What equity do you need to call?
d-l3-odds-q5.explanation: Call 5BB and the total pot after your call is 15BB + 5BB = 20BB, so the equity you need is 5/20 = 25%. Expressed as pot odds, "amount you can win : amount you call = 15:5 = 3:1", whose break-even equity is 1/(3+1) = 25% — the same number either way.

d-l3-odds-q6.question: A gutshot (4 outs) from Flop to River hits about how often?
d-l3-odds-q6.explanation: 4 outs with the 2/4 rule: 4×4=16%. Actual about 16.5%. A gutshot needs great implied odds to call.

d-l3-odds-q7.question: Pot is 35BB, you need to call 15BB. You have a flush draw (9 outs) — what should you do?
d-l3-odds-q7.explanation: Calling 15BB wins 35BB, needing 15/50=30% equity. But a flush draw only has about 19% turn-to-river equity — not enough. Fold.

d-l3-odds-q8.scenario: Flop, you have a combo draw
d-l3-odds-q8.question: A flush draw + OESD (15 outs) from Flop to River hits about how often?
d-l3-odds-q8.explanation: 15 outs with the 2/4 rule: 15×4=60%, but actual about 54%. A combo draw is very strong — over 50% equity.
